item.title: Police constable recruitment: Vacancies increase, competition decreases
item.description:
Bangladesh Police has received 102,694 applications for the ongoing recruitment of Trainee Recruit Constables (TRC). Although the recruitment circular was published on 9 October and applications closed on 30 October, it did not specify the number of vacancies.

However, there is now a strong possibility that 6,000 constables will eventually be recruited through this process, despite the absence of a confirmed vacancy figure in the initial announcement.

Although the number of applicants is lower than in the previous recruitment drive, the possibility of recruiting up to three times as many constables could make the competition less intense, officials concerned say.

Kamarum Munira, assistant inspector general (Media and Public Relations) at Police Headquarters, confirmed the overall recruitment figures. She told Prothom Alo that a total of 102,694 jobseekers from across the country had applied online under the ongoing recruitment circular.

Explaining the proposed recruitment numbers, Kamarum Munira said there are currently 2,000 vacant constable posts in the police force. Meanwhile, a proposal to recruit 10,000 new constables has been sent to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

Considering the approval process, the plan is to recruit 4,000 additional constables from the proposed 10,000 posts, alongside filling the existing 2,000 vacancies through the current circular. This means a total of 6,000 constables may be recruited in the ongoing process.

The remaining 6,000 posts from the proposed 10,000 will be filled in phases through subsequent recruitment circulars.

A comparison of the two recruitment drives

A comparison of the previous and current constable recruitment circulars shows several clear changes in the level of competition among applicants.

The previous recruitment circular, published in April this year, specified 2,703 constable posts. A total of 126,000 candidates applied for those positions, meaning an average of 47 applicants competed for each post.

In contrast, the current circular, published on 9 October, did not initially mention the number of vacancies. After the application process ended on October 30, a total of 102,694 applications had been received.

If the number of posts increases to 6,000 with the addition of vacancies from Police Headquarters, an average of just 17 candidates will compete for each position.

In other words, the number of applicants has fallen by around 23,000 compared with the previous recruitment drive. At the same time, the number of posts is likely to increase from 2,703 to 6,000.

As a result, candidates may have a much greater chance of securing a position in the police force than in previous recruitment drives.

Pledge of transparency at every stage

The government is emphasising the recruitment of young and skilled personnel to ensure public safety and improve the quality of services at the field level. However, regardless of the number of applicants, candidates must meet the required academic, physical and institutional qualifications to qualify for final selection.

According to the recruitment circular, candidates will have to pass several rigorous stages to be selected on merit. Their initial eligibility will first be assessed through preliminary screening. Qualified candidates will then undergo physical measurement and the Physical Endurance Test (PET), followed by a written examination and a psychological test.

Police Headquarters has issued a strict warning to ensure transparency throughout the recruitment process. No political lobbying, financial transactions or submission of false information will be tolerated beyond merit, physical fitness and eligibility.

If any false information or evidence of fraud is found at any stage of the selection process, the candidate's application will be cancelled immediately and legal action will be taken.

item.title: Garment workers protest by blocking highway in Gazipur, halting traffic
item.description:
Garment factory workers are staging a protest by blocking the Dhaka–Tangail Highway in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair upazila, Gazipur. The demonstration began around 8:30 a.m. today, Saturday, bringing traffic to a standstill on both sides of the highway. The disruption has caused considerable inconvenience to commuters. In response to the situation, several nearby factories have announced temporary closures.

According to factory workers and police sources, workers from two garment factories—Tropical, located in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area of Kaliakair, and Apex Lingerie, in the Purba Chandra area—staged protests last Thursday. That day, police dispersed the workers by firing tear gas shells and sound grenades. Several workers were injured in the incident.

After reports spread that a worker injured during Thursday’s protest had died, workers stopped working and began demonstrating today. At one point, they gathered on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway near their factory in the Chandra Palli Bidyut area and blocked the road.

After receiving reports of the incident, members of the Gazipur Industrial Police, Kaliakair Police Station and Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) arrived at the scene. They are speaking with the workers and trying to restore normalcy. However, tensions escalated as the workers became agitated. The highway blockade has caused severe hardship for commuters. Many have begun walking to their destinations.

Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Mohammad Amzad Hossain said the workers were staging the protest based on rumours that someone had died. However, he said their main demand was an increase in wages. Workers from seven to eight nearby factories had taken to the streets.

item.title: Stench of 'Sandpapergate' set to linger as scandal reignites
item.description:
Australian captain Pat Cummins wants to draw a line under "Sandpapergate" and move on, but the stench of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal is set to linger after a week of sensational accusations and denials.
Cummins held an intense 70-minute press conference on Friday and answered every question thrown at him after former teammate Usman Khawaja reopened old wounds with the release of his explosive autobiography.
In the book, he claimed the whole team, including Cummins, knew about the plot to alter the ball with sandpaper during the Cape Town Test against South Africa.
Only David Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft were held responsible by Cricket Australia for the incident that shattered the nation's reputation, with all three sent home in disgrace and banned.
Cummins repeated multiple times that he was not aware of the plan, insisting Khawaja's version of events was "100 percent wrong".
"I don't want to talk about this again after today ... because at some point we've got to move on," he added.
His plea drew support from Justin Langer, who took over as head coach when Darren Lehmann quit in the wake of the scandal.
"Hopefully, that will put some sort of line in the sand because we have to move on," Langer told SEN radio.
"There's too many people being hurt in Australian cricket ... and that includes the Australian public.
"When I talk about Australian cricket, it's about the public, it's about the fans, it's about the players, it's about everyone who's involved: the past players, the present players, future players. We have to draw a line in the sand somewhere."
Another former Test great Greg Chappell also urged an end to the in-fighting.
"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," he told reporters.
"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket."
While calls to put the issue to bed mount, it could blow up again with several key players yet to comment, notably Smith and Bancroft, while Khawaja has media commitments to sell his book.
Warner, who has strongly backed close friend Khawaja's new version of events, made clear he will not rest "until the truth is out there".
- Pick your side -
"The biggest error of the Cummins Q and A was his belief that his appearance would allow everyone to draw a line under the affair and move on," national broadcaster ABC said in an analysis.
"That's not happening. We're dealing with hurt feelings here, fractured relationships and bruised egos and nebulous concepts of truth and justice.
"You better pick your side, if you haven't already, because this is never going away."
Whether what really happened is ever properly established remains to be seen with Cricket Australia adamant it will not be re-opening its investigation.
But the bonds of a 15-year friendship between Cummins, Khawaja and Warner have splintered.
Cummins accused Khawaja of being "flippant and casual" by dropping his bombshell claims eight years after the fact, suggesting some of them were "probably defamatory".
That prompted Warner to blast Cummins for throwing Khawaja "under the bus" and The Australian newspaper to declare that "a generation of Australian players is officially at war".
Cummins insists unity within the current Australian team, which includes Smith, remains strong despite the week's firestorm as they prepare for a home Test series against New Zealand in December-January.
He said he had spoken to Smith, who lost the captaincy and was banned for a year over "Sandpapergate", and suggested the veteran batsman was keen not to regurgitate the past.
"I have spoken to Smithy. Without breaking confidence, he is done with this, he wants to move on," said Cummins.
"This was very traumatic for him. If standing up today and answering all your questions helps everyone move on, then maybe it's a good thing."

item.title: Tearful Pochettino admits Man Utd move is one of his toughest decisions
item.description:
Mauricio Pochettino said Friday that leaving his role as USA boss to take charge of Manchester United was "one of the most difficult" decisions of his career as he prepares for one of football's toughest jobs.
The 54-year-old Argentine fought back tears as he bade an emotional farewell to US football, hours after the Premier League giants announced he would replace the sacked Michael Carrick.
The former Tottenham, Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea boss will take up his new position on November 18, with a monumental task ahead of him.
United have made their worst start to a domestic campaign in 40 years and are languishing in the Premier League relegation zone during the current international break.
Pochettino is understood to have signed a two-and-a-half-year deal at Old Trafford, taking him through to the end of the 2028/29 season.
"We learned a lot from you all, from this amazing country," Pochettino told a media conference in Fayetteville, Georgia. "I think this was one of the most difficult decisions of (my) career."
Pochettino, who led the USA to the last 16 at this year's World Cup, will oversee back-to-back CONCACAF Nations League matches against Haiti on Saturday and next Tuesday before leaving for England.
He said he had not considered a possible return to the Premier League when he signed a contract extension with US Soccer in August, but added the opportunity to join United was too good to turn down.
"I never said I wanted to go back in the Premier League," he said. "Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives."
US Soccer CEO and secretary general JT Batson said Pochettino had left a lasting legacy through his "leadership, professionalism and commitment to our players and culture".
The federation is reportedly set to receive around $10 million in compensation, plus more to cover the departure of Pochettino's coaching staff.
United said in a statement that Pochettino was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".
"Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues," the club added.
The 20-time English champions are one of the giants of world football but have largely been also-rans since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.
Pochettino is the eighth permanent manager tasked with returning the Red Devils to former glories.
He started his Premier League managerial career with Southampton before joining Tottenham, where he never finished lower than fifth during his five full seasons in charge and also reached the 2019 Champions League final.
Pochettino claimed the first trophies of his managerial career with PSG, collecting the 2021 French Cup and 2022 Ligue 1 title, but did not see out his contract in Paris.
He returned to the dugout at Chelsea in 2023 but only lasted one season.
The former Argentina defender, who has been linked with the United job on several previous occasions, faces a baptism of fire at the home of fierce rivals Liverpool on November 22.
He must unite a club that is deeply divided on and off the pitch.
United captain Bruno Fernandes was dropped last month after he criticised Carrick's tactics and Lisandro Martinez took a public swipe at the United hierarchy over a lack of investment.
Angry fans vented their frustration at the club's ownership following the sacking of the popular Carrick, who won multiple trophies as a player.
Despite fierce and persistent protests over two decades, the US-based Glazer family still hold a majority stake in United, which Malcolm Glazer bought via a leveraged takeover in 2005, saddling the club with huge debts.
Any hopes the arrival of British billionaire Jim Ratcliffe as a minority owner in 2024 would signal a new dawn have since faded.
Carrick issued an emotional statement Friday wishing United "nothing but success", adding that his love for the club "never dies".

item.title: The miracle cure in your Facebook feed is killing Bangladeshis
item.description:
Every Bangladeshi family knows the scene. My father is newly diagnosed with diabetes. The doctor's advice is the same as always: Medication, diet, regular monitoring, lifelong discipline. It is sound advice, and it is exhausting to follow.
Then his morning walk friend forwards a video to him. A man in a white coat promises a cure in seven days, with no injections and no side effects, for only Tk3,500 and cash on delivery.
This is not harmless chatter. It is a business, and its customers are dying.
Diabetes is a lifelong condition for which no cure currently exists. That inconvenient truth is the foundation of a thriving commercial ecosystem on Facebook and TikTok: Fake doctors, unregistered supplements, and "miracle" pills sold to people who are frightened, tired, or simply priced out of regular care.
Social media is filled with products claiming to replace insulin or conventional medication with herbal alternatives, despite no credible scientific evidence supporting those claims. Patients each month require hospitalization after following unqualified health advice found on social media and resulting in liver, kidney, or cardiovascular complications.
Think about what that number means. Families continue to pay for someone else's marketing copy with their organs. Now think about the patients who never made it to a hospital.
The word "herbal" does a great deal of the sellers' work. In a country with a long and respected tradition of traditional remedies, "natural" feels "safe." It is not.
A product with no declared dose, no tested purity, and no registration is simply an unknown substance. The danger is greatest when a patient stops a prescribed drug because a post told them they no longer need it.
What makes this scam distinctly Bangladeshi is how skilfully it borrows trust. Fraudsters know we respect the doctor, the professor, and the familiar newspaper masthead, so they counterfeit all three.
Dr Jahangir Kabir, a prominent health advocate who promotes lifestyle-based approaches to diabetes, has said dishonest groups are misusing his name to sell unregulated medicines.
He reports that hundreds of fake Facebook pages were created in his name, some even mimicking his verified profile's blue-badge image. A man who tells people to change how they eat and live found his face on the label of a bottle.
He is not alone. Microbiologist Dr Senjuti Saha discovered that her name and image were being used in a fraudulent campaign and filed a general diary at the police station.
Dismislab traced the "Optimax" diabetes product to counterfeit pages mimicking Prothom Alo, featuring fake interviews with "prominent" Bangladeshi professionals.
Even the health minister's identity has been hijacked: iIn 2024 the ministry had to warn that fake Facebook accounts were being opened in his name, with advertisements that could cheat the public.
When the scammer can wear the face of a trusted doctor and the logo of a trusted newspaper, "just don't believe everything online" is not advice. It is an abdication.
We have long assumed that more smartphones meant more awareness. The evidence is more troubling. Studies suggest that mobile phone ownership is associated with greater exposure to misinformation, not just greater access to information.
In a country where phones have reached the village before the specialist has, the same device that delivers a telemedicine consultation also delivers a "cure" for diabetes. In many cases, it is the second that arrives first.
Self-medication was already common long before Facebook. We buy tablets over the counter, trust a neighbour's prescription, and stretch a doctor's visit as far as it will go. Influencers did not create this habit. They have simply learned to monetize it.
Media professionals are not blameless. For years our response to health misinformation has been the occasional "myth-buster" column, published once, read by few, and forgotten by the next news cycle. The scammers publish daily. We cannot answer a daily campaign with an annual correction.
Newspapers need standing health fact-check desks, with trained reporters, a medical advisory panel, and the same institutional seriousness we give to political fact-checking. A fake diabetes ad should be treated with the same urgency as a fake political quote.
Television channels and online portals should produce short, shareable "spot the scam" segments in Bangla. Sixty seconds are enough to show a viewer how to check whether a doctor is registered with the Bangladesh Medical and Dental Council, why "cure in seven days" is a warning rather than a promise, and why no pill replaces insulin. Content that is easy to forward to the family WhatsApp group is how we compete on the scammers' own ground.
We should use AI sensibly. Newsrooms can deploy language tools, including Bangla-capable ones, to flag viral health claims, repeated ad creatives, and suspicious pages at a scale no human desk can match.
But AI should only flag. Verification, context, and the final call must remain with trained editors and doctors. A machine can tell us where the fire is. It cannot tell us whether the person in the video is really a physician.
Finally, the media must stop accepting the framing that this is merely a "content moderation" problem. Content moderation means a platform deciding whether a post stays up.
What we are describing is the sale of unregistered medicinal products, under false identities, to sick people, for profit. That is consumer fraud and a public health offense.
The Directorate General of Drug Administration, the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission, the consumer rights authorities and law enforcement all have a role.
So do Meta and TikTok, which earn revenue from the very advertisements that deceive our citizens.
The press should keep asking the uncomfortable questions: Who approved this ad, who was paid, who was prosecuted, and how many times was it reported before it came down?
The next time a "miracle cure" appears in your feed, remember what it is: Someone's sales pitch, aimed at your parent's fear.
Insulin is not a conspiracy, and diabetes does not end in seven days. The sooner we say so, loudly, every single day, the fewer families will learn it in a hospital corridor.
Dewan Shahnoor Alam Sourav is a lecturer in the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB). Can be reached at ds.alam.sourav@gmail.com .

item.title: How do I grieve someone I have not met yet?
item.description:
This is what I kept asking myself as I waited in the hospital, knowing that my 4.5-month pregnancy was coming to an end. Perhaps it is simply human nature to grow attached to the life growing inside you.
My entire life, I have catastrophized everything. The same happened when I found out I was pregnant. But I quickly tried to quiet that part of me and focus on doing my best.
Everything was going perfectly. I had no known risk factors, my scans had gone well, and my doctor had told me to schedule an appointment for the following month.
No one had warned me that even when everything seemed to be going well, it could all turn upside down in the blink of an eye.
I had gone to sleep when my amniotic fluid ruptured. Even half asleep, I knew what that meant. My pregnancy had ended. I was rushed to the hospital, and the duty doctor tried to console me: “We do not know yet.”
But I knew that the future I had already started imagining would no longer come to be.
I had to wait an excruciating 12 hours for my gynaecologist to examine me. She finally explained what would happen next. I would be given one dose of medication that day and more the following day to induce labour.
Miscarriage . Just one word, carrying a weight that is almost impossible to put into words. A grief so profound, yet one no one warns you about.
While I waited in the hospital for the procedures to be completed, my aunts, uncles, grandmothers, cousins, everyone, rallied around me. I was going through one of the most difficult periods of my life, but I was wrapped in a blanket of love.
The women around me told me their own stories of loss, their struggles, and how they had found a way through. Even though my own pain felt insurmountable, it was the strength I found in their stories that helped me through.
Despite medical science coming such a long way, no reason could be identified for why this was happening to me. The pregnancy was not advanced enough for there to be any hope of saving it, but it was also not early enough for my miscarriage to go unnoticed.
The medication I was given sent my body into what felt like a state of shock. I was shivering uncontrollably, and when the shivering stopped, my body would have to endure contractions. I had to feel the pain of labour, but there was no baby to hold at the end of it.
Nothing could be done to ease my pain, knowing that there was no possibility of a different ending. I was handed a death certificate for someone who never even had a birth certificate.
It is estimated that one in four to six pregnancies ends in miscarriage. But the statistics are complex. There are a multitude of factors that can play a role.
Most of the websites I have visited state that miscarriages are common. And this makes me question: Why is there so little conversation about something that affects women so deeply?
A pregnancy loss is deeply personal, and it should always be a woman’s prerogative to decide whether she wants to talk about it. But for those who do want to talk about it, do we have enough safe spaces?
There is so little mental health support for women going through a loss like this. I was genuinely grateful for the hospital staff who consoled me, who held my hand when my body was going through unbearable pain, and for the doctors who treated me with respect and dignity. But is that guaranteed for every woman who experiences a loss like this?
Too often, these losses are minimised with statements such as, “It was not meant to be.” As though a few words can make the grief disappear. We should hold space for women who are going through these losses and create more meaningful systems of support.
When even “rich” countries struggle to fund research into miscarriage and pregnancy loss, there is little hope for a country like Bangladesh.
The world can be an extremely cruel place for women. But I refuse to be anything but kind to myself.
There was a version of me that existed before the miscarriage, and there is a version of me that exists now. I do not think they are the same person.
The trivial things in life that used to bother me no longer seem to matter. Things I once thought were important have suddenly lost weight. There is something about losing something so deeply wanted that changes your understanding of what truly matters.
While I do not want my pregnancy loss to define me, I also cannot pretend that it is not a part of who I am now. I will carry this loss with me, and I will not allow it to be swept under the carpet or reduced to something that simply happened and should be forgotten.
I am still grieving the future I do not get to have. There is no linear path through a loss this profound. I was applauded for being brave, but the truth is, I was forced to be brave.
I no longer want to be courageous. I want to mourn. I want to grieve the life I never got to meet, on my own terms.
It is the strength of my parents, partner, and siblings that has kept me going. Life keeps moving forward, even though it felt like mine had stopped for a while.
The only lesson I carry forward is that I will show up with love, strength, and support for any woman who has gone through something similar. There should be more conversations about this reality, about a kind of loss that can be so profound and yet have no logical answers. Women should be allowed to grieve without being told how they should grieve.
Ahona Hassan is a human rights activist passionate about speaking on issues often left unspoken.
